claims.text: Greg Short asserts that internal self-talk — the no's an entrepreneur tells themselves — is the true barrier of entry to any business challenge, not external rejection. When a business is not growing after six months of effort, the entrepreneur typically blames external conditions or outside resistance, but the operative constraint is the inner dialogue that decided the path was closed before external forces even weighed in.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies to founders who have tried for roughly six months and concluded the path is not for them
Applies when the business is still not growing (demand or execution constraint unresolved)
claims.mechanism: The inner dialogue forecloses action before external rejection occurs; because the entrepreneur has already decided the answer is no, they stop the behaviors that would produce growth, making the internal no self-fulfilling.
bounded_by: Greg Short distinguishes this from cases where external parties are the actual source of the block — he treats those separately

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that when the barrier is genuinely external — another person or institution saying no — the correct response is persistent financial or relational pressure (in his words, 'put your money where your mouth is and just pay them until they say yes'), because external no's are negotiable whereas self-imposed no's require internal recognition first.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies only when the source of the blocking no is an external person or institution, not the entrepreneur's own inner dialogue
Applies in business contexts where persistent pursuit or payment is a viable lever (e.g., partnership negotiation, vendor relationships, channel access)
claims.mechanism: External rejection is a negotiating position, not a final state; continuous financial or relationship investment changes the other party's incentive structure until agreement becomes their rational choice.
bounded_by: Greg Short frames this only for external resistance; he explicitly contrasts it with internal self-limiting beliefs, which require a different intervention (recognition and questioning)

practices.text: When your business is not growing after sustained effort, audit whether the obstacle is truly external or whether it is an internal narrative — specifically, identify and question the no's you are telling yourself before concluding the opportunity is closed.
When a genuine external party is saying no, do not accept it as final; continue pursuing — including financially — until they say yes, rather than internalizing their resistance as your own limit.
